newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vols catch fire as dlr nosedives.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vols catch fire as dlr nosedives.

text.p: Implied volatilities for shorter dated dollar-pair options surged as the dollar was fiercely sold off in U.S. trading, dealers said.
The dollar, which had closed on Thursday in the mid-123 yen area and above 1.70 marks, plunged to about 119.05 yen and 1.6825 marks.
"It's one of those once-a-year moves," said Masao Okada, chief options dealer at Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank in New York. "It's impossible to really explain why it happens."
He noted that bids and offers in both spot and options thinned out quickly after the dollar's panic selloff.

One-month dollar/yen implied volatility soared to 10.4/10.7 percent from 9.2/9.5 late on Thursday. One-month 25-delta risk reversal -- the put/call pricing differential -- widened to 1.0/1.5 points in favor of yen calls.

Okada said that when the Tokyo market opened today, one-month 120-yen yen call was a fairly deep out-of-the-money 20-delta option. But in a matter of less than a day the dollar broke through that strike level.
Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc, noted that many bank dealers had become short in downside strike prices this week after a surge in end-users' yen call buying.
For those who had not immediately turned to the market to hedge those sales, perhaps in an attempt to capture the weekend time decay, the dollar's freefall today was extremely painful, he said.
"You had very little time," Revercomb said.

A long options position, which has positive gamma, would allow a delta-neutral dealer to buy dollars when spot goes down and sell them when the currency goes higher. But those negative gamma positions in the downside strikes forced dealers to sell dollars at lower levels, at an accelerating rate, as spot fell.
"What this means is nobody is going to want to be short, particularly have uncontained gamma, even though volatilities might creep up to tempting levels," Revercomb said.
"I think you'll continue to see upward pressure on volatilities because it's gone from looking like a correction to looking like a turning point in the dollar," he added.

Traders noted that because of a fairly long period of steady rise in the dollar, a lot of Japanese exporter companies still had a lot of unhedged dollar exposure and insurance firms had not really hedged their increased dollar investments.
Hedge funds were also likely to unwind their dollar investment funded with yen borrowings, they added.
Back-end volatilities have so far been slow to react, but Revercomb expected demand to move up the curve once the actual volatility calms down to levels that cannot justify the front-end implieds.
In dollar/mark, which was basically tracking dollar/yen, one-month volatility rose about 0.7 point to 9.2/9.4 percent.
"This has turned into an overall dollar move," Revercomb said. "I think you'll see more people coming in looking to buy that (dollar/mark volatility) as a way to jump on the train."
